This review companion follows the headings in **Table discussion.pdf** (seven
pages, supplied November 10, 2026).
These examples reproduce the available reporting layouts with newly simulated
illustrative results, rather than the teams' original numerical results or
visual styling. HTML output uses gt when installed, including native column
spanners and row sections. Missing features
are flagged beside the corresponding example for a separate implementation step.

Load `crmPack` and set the display options used throughout this document.
Tables use `gt` when it is installed and the output is HTML; otherwise they use
`kable`. The code chunks are shown together with their results.

```{r reporting-setup}
library(crmPack)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE,
    comment = "#>",
    message = FALSE,
    error = FALSE,
    fig.width = 7,
    fig.height = 5,
    fig.path = "reporting-simulation-results-figures/"
)
report_format <- if (
    requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()
) {
    "gt"
} else {
    "kable"
}
```

Save generated figures under a directory specific to this review document.

```{r review-figures}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = "table-discussion-review-figures/")
```

Define an illustrative single-agent trial with doses of 50, 100, 200 and 400
and a target dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) probability of 20–35%. The logistic
model supplies the prior. `NextBestNCRM` chooses doses subject to a 25% upper
limit on the posterior probability of overdosing. Patients enter in cohorts
of three, starting at 50, and dose increases are limited to 100%.

The trial stops when the lowest dose is judged unsafe, no dose is admissible,
or at least 18 patients have been treated. The labels assigned here are reused
in the reporting tables. The short MCMC settings keep this example manageable;
a study analysis requires adequate sampling and convergence assessment.

```{r reporting-design}
empty_data <- Data(doseGrid = c(50, 100, 200, 400))
target <- c(0.20, 0.35)
model <- LogisticLogNormal(
    mean = c(-0.85, 1),
    cov = matrix(c(1, -0.5, -0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
    ref_dose = 200
)
design <- Design(
    model = model,
    nextBest = NextBestNCRM(
        target = target,
        overdose = c(target[2], 1),
        max_overdose_prob = 0.25
    ),
    stopping = StoppingLowestDoseHSRBeta(
        target = target[2],
        prob = 0.90,
        report_label = "Lowest dose unsafe"
    ) |
        StoppingMissingDose(report_label = "No admissible dose") |
        StoppingMinPatients(nPatients = 18, report_label = "Maximum sample size"),
    increments = IncrementsRelative(intervals = 0, increments = 1),
    cohort_size = CohortSizeConst(3),
    data = empty_data,
    startingDose = 50
)
mcmc_options <- McmcOptions(burnin = 100, step = 1, samples = 500)
```

Draw samples from the model with no observed patients, so these are prior
samples. Setting the seed makes the example reproducible. The same samples
are reused for the prior plots and summary table.

```{r reporting-prior-samples}
set.seed(966)
prior_samples <- mcmc(empty_data, model, mcmc_options)
```

Specify six possible true toxicity profiles, one row per scenario and one
column per dose. These probabilities describe the data-generating assumptions
for the simulations; they are separate from the model's prior beliefs.
Interpolate each row into a function of dose, then collect the functions and
target interval in a `ToxicityScenarios` object for reporting.

```{r reporting-truths}
true_probabilities <- list(
    "T1 (First)" = c(0.30, 0.45, 0.50, 0.55),
    "T2 (Early)" = c(0.25, 0.30, 0.45, 0.50),
    "T3 (Late)" = c(0.05, 0.17, 0.30, 0.45),
    "T4 (Last)" = c(0.17, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30),
    "T5 (Safe)" = c(0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10),
    "T6 (Toxic)" = c(0.45, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60)
)
truth_functions <- lapply(
    true_probabilities,
    function(prob) {
        # rule = 2 ensures that the function returns the value at the
        # min and max grid point, respectively, for out-of-bounds doses
        approxfun(empty_data@doseGrid, prob, rule = 2)
    }
)
truths <- ToxicityScenarios(
    scenarios = truth_functions,
    dose_grid = empty_data@doseGrid,
    target = target
)
```

Create three hypothetical trial snapshots at the starting dose: zero, one,
or three DLTs among three patients. Evaluate each snapshot with `scenario()`
to obtain posterior summaries and the design's next-dose or stopping decision.
Retain these evaluations for the trial-realizations table below.

```{r reporting-data-evaluate}
hypothetical_data <- list(
    "3 patients, 0 DLTs" = Data(
        x = rep(50, 3),
        y = c(0, 0, 0),
        doseGrid = empty_data@doseGrid
    ),
    "3 patients, 1 DLT" = Data(
        x = rep(50, 3),
        y = c(0, 0, 1),
        doseGrid = empty_data@doseGrid
    ),
    "3 patients, 3 DLTs" = Data(
        x = rep(50, 3),
        y = c(1, 1, 1),
        doseGrid = empty_data@doseGrid
    )
)
set.seed(968)
evaluated_data <- lapply(hypothetical_data, function(data) {
    scenario(design, data = data, mcmcOptions = mcmc_options)
})
```

Simulate 10 trials under each of the six true toxicity profiles, using the
same design and a separate reproducible seed for each scenario. This small
simulation count demonstrates the reporting interface; reliable operating
characteristics require many more trials. `SimulationsSummaryList` collects
the results and summarizes them relative to the target interval. Subsequent
operating-characteristics tables and plots reuse these results.

```{r reporting-simulate}
#| cache: true
nsim <- 10L
simulations <- lapply(truth_functions, function(truth_fun) {
    simulate(
        design,
        truth = truth_fun,
        nsim = nsim,
        seed = 970,
        mcmcOptions = mcmc_options,
        parallel = FALSE
    )
})
oc <- SimulationsSummaryList(simulations, target = target)
```

# Bayer

## Prior definition plot

PDF p. 2: mean and 95% prior credible interval with optional target overlay.

Plot the prior mean toxicity probability and its 95% credible interval across
doses. Overlay the target interval to show how the prior relates to the
study's desired toxicity range.

```{r reporting-prior-plot}
plot(
    prior_samples,
    model,
    empty_data,
    statistic = "mean",
    level = 0.95,
    target = target
)
```

*Question:* Is this ok as is or do we want the option to highlight the specific doses on the dose grid / the points that belong to them?

## Prior random draws plot

PDF p. 2: 100 curves drawn from the same prior samples.

Display 100 sampled prior dose–toxicity curves to show the variability in
plausible relationships before observing patients. The plotting seed fixes
which curves are selected from the existing prior samples.

```{r reporting-prior-draws}
plot_prior_draws(prior_samples, model, empty_data, n = 100, seed = 967)
```

## Scenario definition table

PDF pp. 2–3, Table 10-3: the six probability rows are transcribed from the notes.

Render the six true toxicity profiles as a table, rounding probabilities to
two decimal places. These are the simulation inputs, not estimated results.

```{r reporting-truth-table}
report_table(truths, digits = 2)
```

## Scenario definition plot

PDF p. 3, Figure 10-1: the same probabilities, with the study's target band.

Plot the same six true profiles against dose, with the target interval for
reference. This makes it easier to compare where each scenario lies relative
to the desired toxicity range. This works because `truths` is a `ToxicityScenarios` object, which the plotting function can interpret correctly.

```{r reporting-truth-plot}
plot(truths)
```

## Operating characteristics table

PDF pp. 3–4: native row sections, supplied stopping-rule labels, selections, correct selections, sample-size
summaries, patients above target, and per-dose patients/DLTs. Per-dose SDs are
shown using the requested mean (SD) option.

First we wrap the list of simulation results into a `SimulationsSummaryList` object, which organizes the data for subsequent reporting.
Build an overview from the existing simulations, reporting stopping reasons
under the labels defined in the design. Select the statistics, assign readable
labels and row sections, and show per-dose counts as mean (SD). Sample-size
summaries also include the range and 10th/90th percentiles. Render the result
with the selected table engine; for `gt`, display row-group labels in a column.
The default `stop_categories = NULL` retains the supplied stopping-rule labels.
Grouped rows automatically omit the statistic prefix, so the stop reasons
appear under their supplied labels without additional overrides. Dose selection
shows `None` first, followed by the dose values without a repeated prefix. Optional
individual renaming uses a nested list, for example
`labels = list(prop_stop_by_label = c("Lowest dose unsafe" = "Unsafe"))`.
Stop rows count rule activations and can overlap, so their percentages need
not sum to 100.

```{r reporting-bayer}
bayer_oc <- SimulationsSummaryList(
    simulations,
    target = target
)
bayer <- report_oc_overview(
    bayer_oc,
    stats = c(
        "prop_stop_by_label",
        "dose_selection",
        "prop_mtd_correct",
        "n_pat_mean_sd",
        "n_pat_minmax",
        "n_pat_quantiles",
        "n_above_target_mean_sd",
        "n_pat_per_dose",
        "n_dlt_per_dose"
    ),
    sd = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9),
    labels = list(
        dose_selection = c(none = "None"),
        n_pat_mean_sd = "Mean (SD)",
        n_pat_minmax = "Min–max",
        n_pat_quantiles = "10th/90th percentiles"
    ),
    row_groups = c(
        prop_stop_by_label = "Stop reason (%)",
        dose_selection = "Dose selection (%)",
        prop_mtd_correct = "Correct dose selected (%)",
        n_pat_mean_sd = "Total patients",
        n_pat_minmax = "Total patients",
        n_pat_quantiles = "Total patients",
        n_above_target_mean_sd = "Patients above target",
        n_pat_per_dose = "Patients per dose, mean (SD)",
        n_dlt_per_dose = "DLTs per dose, mean (SD)"
    ),
    title = "Bayer-style operating characteristics",
    spanner = sprintf("%d trials per scenario; target 20–35%%", nsim)
)
bayer_table <- report_table(bayer, format = report_format)
if (report_format == "gt") {
    bayer_table <- gt::tab_options(bayer_table, row_group.as_column = TRUE)
}
bayer_table
```

Additional available customization: above-target min/max and quantiles via
`OCStat`, using the cached summary.

Define two custom `OCStat` summaries for the number of patients treated above
the target interval: the range and the 10th/90th percentiles. Both use the
cached per-trial summary values. Add them alongside the built-in mean (SD)
and render a markdown table without rerunning the simulations.

```{r reporting-custom}
above_range <- OCStat(
    label = "Patients above target, min–max",
    fun = function(sims, summary, scenario) range(summary@n_above_target),
    format = "[%.0f–%.0f]"
)
above_quantiles <- OCStat(
    label = "Patients above target, 10th/90th percentiles",
    fun = function(sims, summary, scenario) {
        quantile(summary@n_above_target, c(0.1, 0.9), names = FALSE)
    },
    format = "[%.1f–%.1f]"
)
report_oc_overview(
    oc,
    stats = list(
        "n_above_target_mean_sd",
        range = above_range,
        quantiles = above_quantiles
    ),
    format = "kable"
)
```

**Flagged for later:** the special "highest planned dose safe" outcome needs a
rule-based definition and is not a synonym for highest-dose selection. Duration
mean/SD exists for `DASimulations` with recorded durations; this example has no
elapsed time. Cohort-scaled duration and duration min/max/quantiles are not
provided by the current registry. The notes' five particular stop reasons also
require a design containing those rules; this example has toxicity, no-admissible-dose, and
maximum-size rules. Above-target distribution summaries use custom
statistics rather than built-in min/max and quantile entries.

## Plots

PDF pp. 4–5: selection percentages and patient counts.

Plot the percentage of trials selecting each dose for each true scenario,
arranging the scenario panels in two columns.

```{r reporting-selection-plot}
plot(oc, type = "doseSelected", ncol = 2)
```

Plot patient allocation by dose for each true scenario, using the same
simulation summary and two-column panel layout.

```{r reporting-patients-plot}
plot(oc, type = "nPatients", ncol = 2)
```

The PDF's per-dose patient-count boxplots and violin
plots are shown below through `plot_type`. The PDF's BOIN comparison and
true-rate annotation strip are not reproduced by these CRM reporting plots.

Show the distribution of per-dose patient counts across simulated trials
with boxplots and then violin plots. Both views use the same trial results.

```{r reporting-patient-distributions}
plot(oc, type = "nPatients", plot_type = "boxplot", ncol = 2)
plot(oc, type = "nPatients", plot_type = "violin", ncol = 2)
```

**Flagged for later:** a native comparison across different designs and a
true-rate annotation strip for these plots.

# Boehringer

## Summary of Prior Table

PDF pp. 5–6, Tables 9–10: interval probabilities, mean, SD and quantiles.
Columns follow the PDF order: interval probabilities, mean, SD, quantiles.
The interval and quantile columns have native gt spanners.
Here intervals match the illustrative study's 20–35% target; the PDF uses
16–33%. This is a single-arm prior table.

Summarize the prior toxicity probability at each dose with its mean, SD,
2.5th/50th/97.5th percentiles and probabilities of falling below, within or
above the target interval. The interval boundaries are 0, 0.20, 0.35 and 1.
Render the table with three decimal places.

```{r reporting-prior-table}
prior_table <- report_prob_summary(
    prior_samples,
    model,
    empty_data,
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975),
    intervals = c(0, target, 1)
)
report_table(prior_table, format = report_format, digits = 3)
```

**Flagged for later:** one native multi-arm/combination prior table matching
both screenshots is not supported by `report_prob_summary()`.

## Hypothetical Data Scenarios aka Trial Realizations Table

PDF p. 6, Table 13: actual `scenario()` evaluations of three trial snapshots.
The last snapshot illustrates a stopping decision.

Turn the three retained hypothetical-data evaluations into a table of
observations and proposed-dose interval probabilities. Label the underdosing,
target and overdosing probabilities as P(UDS), P(TDS) and P(ODS), respectively,
and display them to three decimal places.

```{r reporting-data-table}
data_table <- report_data_scenarios(
    evaluated_data,
    probabilities = c("underdosing", "target", "overdose")
)
report_table(
    data_table,
    format = report_format,
    probability_labels = c(
        underdosing = "P(UDS)",
        target = "P(TDS)",
        overdose = "P(ODS)"
    ),
    digits = 3
)
```

The reporter supports combination and hierarchical `DataScenario` objects,
including arm names. Native spanners group observed data and proposed-dose
interval probabilities. `NextBestNCRM` now calculates underdose probability
from the same posterior draws, so all three interval probabilities are shown.
**Flagged for later:** the exact two-arm scenario from the notes.

## Scenario Definition Table

PDF p. 6, Table 14: single-agent counterpart using the shared six true scenarios.

Render the same six true toxicity profiles for the Boehringer layout, this
time using the selected table engine and three decimal places.

```{r review-bi-truth-table}
report_table(truths, format = report_format, digits = 3)
```

**Flagged for later:** arm-specific and combination true-toxicity grids are
not supported by `ToxicityScenarios`.

## Operating characteristics Table

PDF p. 6, Table 15: selection classifications, no recommendation, mean and
min/max sample sizes and DLT counts.

Select percentages of under-target, correct, over-target and absent final
dose recommendations, together with mean and range summaries for patients
and DLTs. Transpose the overview so that scenarios appear in rows before
rendering the table.

```{r reporting-bi}
bi <- report_oc_overview(
    oc,
    stats = c(
        "prop_mtd_under",
        "prop_mtd_correct",
        "prop_mtd_over",
        "prop_mtd_none",
        "n_pat_mean",
        "n_pat_minmax",
        "n_dlt_mean",
        "n_dlt_minmax"
    ),
    labels = c(prop_mtd_none = "No final recommendation (%)"),
    title = "BI-style operating characteristics"
)
report_table(report_transpose(bi), format = report_format)
```

**Flagged for later:** hierarchical OC arm subcolumns and paired mean
(min–max) cells. `report_transpose()` now places scenarios in rows, with
separate mean and range columns. No-recommendation
percentage is computed directly, rather than by adding overlapping stop rules.

# Merck

## Operating characteristics overview table

PDF pp. 6–7: six PMDA-style metrics. The joint maximum-size/no-recommendation
statistic uses the public `OCStat` extension interface to match the row meaning.
The built-in maximum-size stopping percentage alone would also count trials
with an MTD recommendation.

Define a custom percentage that counts trials satisfying both conditions:
the maximum-sample-size rule was activated and no final MTD was recommended.
Combine it with mean patient and DLT counts, toxicity stopping, correct
selection and over-target selection to produce the six-metric overview.

```{r reporting-pmda}
max_without_mtd <- OCStat(
    label = "Maximum patients without MTD (%)",
    fun = function(sims, summary, scenario) {
        100 * mean(sims@stop_report[, "Maximum sample size"] & is.na(sims@doses))
    },
    format = "%.1f"
)
pmda <- report_oc_overview(
    oc,
    stats = list(
        "n_pat_mean",
        "n_dlt_mean",
        "prop_stop_tox",
        "prop_mtd_correct",
        max_without_mtd = max_without_mtd,
        "prop_mtd_over"
    ),
    title = "Merck / PMDA-style overview",
    spanner = sprintf("Simulation results: %d trials; target 20–35%%", nsim)
)
report_table(pmda, format = report_format)
```

## Operating characteristics detail table

PDF p. 7: dose columns, scenario groups, counts, selection, true P(DLT), and
SUM/STOP/MAX. SUM uses per-trial totals for count rows. STOP/MAX count terminal
rule activations, can overlap with recommendations, and need not make the row
sum to 100%. This is the current API's meaning, which reviewers should assess
against their desired reporting convention.

Build a detailed operating-characteristics table with dose columns and
scenario groups. Request SDs for per-dose patient and DLT counts, assign
readable count labels, and render the result with the selected table engine.

```{r reporting-merck}
merck <- report_oc_detail(
    oc,
    sd = TRUE,
    labels = c(
        n_dlt_per_dose = "Patients with DLTs, mean (SD)",
        n_pat_per_dose = "Patients, mean (SD)"
    ),
    title = "Merck-style per-dose operating characteristics"
)
report_table(merck, format = report_format)
```

# Additional reporting capabilities

These additions go beyond the screenshot layouts: reversible transposition,
unrounded cell inspection,
automatic column pagination, markdown rendering, and optional gt/Word export.
See the package vignette for export prerequisites.

Transpose the previously constructed prior table to exchange its row and
column layout, then render it without recomputing the prior summaries.

```{r reporting-transpose}
report_table(report_transpose(prior_table), format = report_format)
```

Inspect the first three rows of the PMDA overview as a data frame. Display
the scenario, statistic identifier, unrounded value and formatted text side
by side to see how numerical results relate to the displayed cells.

```{r reporting-raw}
as.data.frame(pmda)[1:3, c("scenario", "stat", "value", "formatted")]
```

Split wide tables into column-sized parts for display. Limit the overview
to four columns per part and the detail table to six, retaining `label` and
`SUM` in each detail part so that split tables keep their row context.

```{r reporting-pagination}
report_table(report_paginate(pmda, max_cols = 4), format = report_format)
report_table(
    report_paginate(merck, max_cols = 6, keep = c("label", "SUM")),
    format = report_format
)
```

Export the overview to Word and the detailed table to HTML using `gt` and
`gt::gtsave()`. The loop exports each paginated overview part to its own Word
file. This chunk is shown but not executed automatically because it writes
files. To run it manually, install `gt` and its Word-export dependency
`rmarkdown`; Word export also requires Pandoc.

```{r reporting-export, eval=FALSE}
report_table(pmda, format = "gt") |> gt::gtsave("overview.docx")
report_table(merck, format = "gt") |> gt::gtsave("detail.html")
parts <- report_table(report_paginate(pmda, max_cols = 4), format = "gt")
for (i in seq_along(parts)) {
    gt::gtsave(parts[[i]], sprintf("overview-%d.docx", i))
}
```
